title: Blessings at home
hookLine: the blessings poem walks into the house: parents, family, and work that isn't chaos

cards: A grandmother's hands, shelling peas at a kitchen table. A dad checking the lock twice before bed. Somebody picking up a parent's prescription on the way home from a long shift.
None of it gets posted. None of it looks like a spiritual life. And yet the Buddha, asked by a god what the highest blessings are, gets to this exact scene a few verses in.
Before meditation, before the deep teachings, the poem stops at home.

teach.b: Here's the verse. Supporting your mother and father. Caring for your partner and your children.
Work that is peaceful, not tangled and chaotic. That is the highest blessing. The text, from its time, says wife and children; some readers today hear it as whoever makes up your household.
Notice the three. Looking up the generations, to parents. Looking across and down, to partner and children.
And the work that feeds them all, done without turmoil. In the Buddha's teaching, caring for parents isn't a small duty.

Elsewhere he says that even carrying your parents on your shoulders for a hundred years wouldn't repay them, though helping them toward goodness and wisdom does. Then the next verse widens the circle. Giving.
Helping your relatives. Actions no one could fault. That is the highest blessing.
And the next. Keeping away from wrongdoing. Holding back from intoxicants.
Being steady and careful in what is good. Listen to how ordinary this is. Pay the bills honestly.
Call your aunt. Don't drink yourself into a mess. Take care of the people who took care of you.
The poem doesn't say these lead to the blessings. It says they are the blessings.

teach.h: NOT THE WAITING ROOM: THE THING ITSELF
teach.b: A tidy, peaceful home, a parent fed, a cousin helped: these are not the waiting room of the spiritual life.
In this poem, they're inside it.

how: The Mangala Sutta is among the protective chants recited at Theravada blessings, and Buddhist teachers draw on its family verses, with the teaching on repaying parents, when they speak about home life.

o: asking your parents' blessing at a wedding
giving your parents' land to a temple

games.q: blessings at home: tap the pairs.

s: the blessings poem places caring for parents among the highest blessings
supporting mother and father opens the home verse.
the poem says family duties come before the real spiritual life starts
it calls these acts the highest blessing in themselves.
holding back from intoxicants is in the list
with keeping away from wrongdoing and steady care in what is good.

games.q: you're busy, and your mother needs her prescription picked up. the blessings poem has a view. what is it?
o: supporting your parents is itself a highest blessing.
it only counts if someone notices.
games.why: the poem names supporting mother and father as the highest blessing, in the same breath as caring for family and peaceful work.

practice: Bring to mind someone in your household or family, a parent, a partner, a child, a cousin, or, if family is complicated for you, the person who has been family to you.
See them doing something ordinary, and notice one thing they do that keeps the household going.

wordCard.voice: Matapitu upatthanam, supporting mother and father. In the Mangala Sutta: caring for partner and children, peaceful work, giving and helping relatives. Not steps toward the blessing: the blessing itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali matapitu upatthanam: supporting, attending to mother and father. the opening of the home verse.

carryVoice: Your line: a blessing. A fed parent, a helped cousin, an honest day's work. Day five hundred ninety-four, done.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 2.4, Mangala Sutta, verses on family, giving and restraint
Anguttara Nikaya 2.33 (Kataññu Sutta): carrying one's parents for a hundred years
